# Playbook for Ref_Auction

When I see a lot's value to me and the current standing bid, I calculate the profit margin (value minus bid) and use that to guide my aggressiveness.

When I'm opening bidding on a lot with no bids yet, I place a modest opening bid rather than passing, since I have private information about the lot's value that others don't.

When the profit margin is substantial (value is significantly higher than the current bid), I bid to stay competitive rather than pass, even if it means raising the bid.

When deciding how much to raise, I use the minimum raise threshold as a floor, not my actual bid. I can and should bid higher than the minimum to be more competitive, especially when the value-to-bid ratio is very favorable.

When I'm in round 2 of a lot and the value is strong, I continue bidding aggressively to secure the lot rather than holding back.

When tracking my budget across the auction, I must keep accurate track of what I've spent and what I have remaining. I should not assume or guess at my budget—I should calculate it precisely from my actual bids. This is critical because my budget display showed an implausibly high number (199,964) that did not match the actual game state.

I should bid to win lots where the value exceeds the standing bid by a meaningful margin, because winning is how I accumulate points. However, I need to distinguish between a truly favorable margin and a marginal one—even with budget to spare, bidding to win a lot worth 11 when I bid 12 gives me only 1 point of profit, which is not worth aggressive play.

When the profit margin is very thin (1 point or less), I should consider passing rather than bidding, especially in later rounds. A thin margin means I'm overpaying relative to my private valuation, which erodes my score.

I should be more conservative on final lots when the margin is slim. Winning with minimal profit is better than losing, but I should not bid more aggressively on final lots if the underlying margin doesn't justify it—the fact that it's the last lot doesn't change the math.

When I notice my budget calculations seem inconsistent with the game's display, I should trust the game's stated budget rather than my own recalculation, as the game has authoritative information about what I've actually spent.

# Auction Playbook

When I see a lot where the value to me exceeds the current bid by a significant margin, I should bid aggressively in round 1 to establish early control, even if it uses up budget quickly.

When I'm deciding whether to bid in round 2, I calculate the profit I'd make (value to me minus the new bid price). If that profit is positive and substantial, I bid to win the lot.

When no one has bid yet on a lot, I make the opening bid at the minimum raise to establish position without overpaying.

When I'm on the final lot and currently behind in score, I bid up to approximately 80-90% of the lot's value to me, since there are no more opportunities to accumulate points afterward.

When I have a small number of wins and other bidders have won multiple lots, I assume the game is close and bid more aggressively on remaining lots to catch up in score.

When the standing bid is well below my valuation, I don't assume my opponents will drop out—I bid expecting the price to climb, and I'm willing to follow it up to my valuation.

When my budget appears to regenerate or behave unexpectedly between bids, I trust the system display rather than my mental arithmetic. The system state is authoritative.

I should track my cumulative score after each lot wins and use that to calibrate my aggression on remaining lots. Winning one lot at a slight loss is acceptable if I can win later lots at strong profits.

I must carefully verify the actual results shown in each round. My mental model of the auction state can diverge from reality—discrepancies between my expected outcome and the actual result shown indicate I misread the situation or other bidders acted unexpectedly. I should update my assumptions when this happens rather than assume a system error.

On interior lots (not the final lot), I should be more selective about chasing bids. A profit of +1 or +2 points on a mid-round lot is thin and not worth aggressive bidding when I should be preserving budget and positioning for later opportunities.

# Auction Playbook

When I see a lot's value to me, I calculate my profit margin as (value - current bid) and use this to guide my bidding decisions.

When the current bid is significantly below my valuation, I bid to enter the competition, but I make minimum-allowed raises rather than jumping aggressively. This preserves budget for remaining lots while keeping me in control.

When I'm in round 1 of 2, I assume round 2 will see higher bids, so I don't overcommit. I make a modest raise that establishes my interest without exhausting my budget preemptively.

When I'm in round 2 of 2 (the final round), I bid more aggressively if the lot still has good value for me, since there's no opportunity to raise again and I want to secure valuable lots.

When I win a lot, I immediately update my remaining budget in my mental accounting and reserve budget for unseen future lots. With 5 lots total, I should not spend more than 20-25% of my budget on any single lot unless it has exceptional value.

When the standing bid approaches my valuation of a lot, I pass rather than bid up into a loss. I only continue bidding if my profit margin (value minus likely final price) remains positive.

When multiple lots are still available and I haven't seen all of them, I avoid getting drawn into bidding wars. I make my raise and accept a pass rather than escalating.

When the estimate of a lot is close to or above what it's worth to me, I'm more cautious and bid smaller amounts or pass entirely, since competitive bidding may push the price past my value threshold.

I will not place bids that would leave me with budget less than 10-15, since this severely constrains my ability to compete on remaining lots.

I must track my actual budget carefully. The display shows my budget after each bid, and I should use that number directly rather than attempting to recalculate from previous state, as system adjustments may occur between rounds that I don't fully observe.

When I calculate remaining budget mid-auction, I should use the most recent budget figure shown to me rather than reconstructing it from earlier bids, to avoid accumulating arithmetic errors.

I should bid even on lots with modest profit margins (under 10) if they are valuable relative to the estimate and I still have healthy budget remaining, as long as the margin is clearly positive and round 2 bidding is unlikely to eliminate it.
